title: Touring the South: train and private homes
summary: On the first Southern trip in 1934 the band lived on the train or in rooms assigned through local committees, with good home cooking.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: You said it depended on what part of the country you were in whether or not you stayed on the train on the siding. Was it generally in the South that you stayed on the -- on the train?

Well, mostly I would say because there were more homes or more hotels and places to stay up in the Northern. And usually when -- the first time we ever went South was in '34, and, of course, we didn't know anything -- anyone down there. And naturally it was easier and cheaper for us to stay on the train than get out and try to find places.
So, in '34 you did stay on the train the whole time?
'34 -- for several years when we made
trips that way where we'd stay mostly on the trains. Were there colored hotels in the South?

I don't know that I would recommend them at that particular time. There were some, but not what -- I wouldn't call them hotels even. Certainly wouldn't want to stay there. And the best thing I thought -- or the best thing we did was hit the job and get on out. Leave. Because accommodations were very poor except in people's homes. There were some beautiful homes.
Was it ever difficult to find private accommodations in homes?

What would happen is that when shows or bands or things were coming in town, they had a sort of a committee that would have the rooms listed -- people that wanted to rent their rooms. And when we got to town usually the agent or whoever it was came down to the train and assigned us to the room to go to, and we went to people's -- different people's homes and stayed that way.
It was a regular network sort of a system --
The next -- the next band that came down, they would do the same thing for them. So, it usually became known that Mrs. so and so has two rooms over there.

Mrs. so and so has three rooms, you know, like that. So, they got along fairly well. And it got so it was real nice because we also usually would eat at the place we stayed. And that was real great because -- some beautiful cooks.
To you knowledge, was there any other band that had its own railroad car like Duke's did?
I don't remember right now. I don't know. I couldn't say.
I've never heard of any other band having one but I --
Yeah. Oh, Cab -- he did the same thing. And there were a few, but just a handful.
